diagnosis.what_is_wrong: The trace shows a sharp change in workload activity, but does not support a kernel-visible resource fault explaining the reported longer coding task. A temporary python3 CPU burst occurs later, but peaks around 0.23 CPU-seconds per wall-second on a four-CPU host; the trace does not show host CPU saturation, and the recorded disk and futex examples do not show meaningful waits.
diagnosis.evidence: Compared the full 03:17:26.200–03:17:59.100 span using process-life findings, the full-trace event-rate aggregations, and per-process sched_stat_runtime. The sharp scheduler/activity decline starts around 03:17:31.5 (switches 807/s at :30 to 8/s at :31.6; wakeups 393/s to 4/s), but it is not evidence by itself of resource exhaustion; the 03:17:33–34 rebound is brief and synchronized across event types. During 03:17:38–54 python3 averages 0.198 CPU-s/s (0.233 CPU-s/s for :42–54), while all processes together average only about 0.23 CPU-s/s against four CPUs. Raw ctf_lines at :30 show a block request completing about 0.8 ms after issue, and sampled futex calls return promptly; these do not support disk wait or futex contention. Process-life shows one pid_ns (4026531836) and persistent core processes rather than a container turnover. The ctf_timeline/query_ctf zero matches were contradicted by the actual DataFrame event counts, so those zeros were not treated as absent activity. I cannot confirm the reported slowdown from this trace alone.
diagnosis.window_evidence: This is the observed workload-transition interval, not a confirmed fault window: per-100-ms scheduler counts collapse starting at 03:17:31.5, followed by persistently lower scheduling rates than 03:17:26–03:17:31 and a temporary python3 runtime rise at 03:17:38–03:17:54. The trace ends at 03:17:59.1, so the later endpoint is the recording boundary; no recovery boundary establishing an incident end was found.
